title: The Latin of the Vulgate

objectives.can: Recognise the features the Vulgate owes to Hebrew and Greek: quia and quoniam for 'that', in with the ablative for instrument, the heavy use of participles, et at the head of every clause, and Hebrew idioms kept word for word.

explanation.summary: The Vulgate is a Latin translation of Hebrew and Greek books, made to follow its originals closely. Because of that, its Latin has habits that Cicero's does not: *et* before almost every clause, *quia* for 'that', a participle where a Roman would write a clause, and Hebrew phrasings carried over word for word. This lesson names those habits and then sends you into Luke 2.

sections.heading: A translation that kept its originals' shape
body: The Latin Bible called the Vulgate was made in the late fourth century, largely by Jerome, from Hebrew for most of the Old Testament and from Greek for the New, and it reuses older Latin versions in parts. Its aim was to give the sense of the original faithfully, and in practice that often meant a close, word-for-word following of the source.

So when a phrase in the Vulgate looks odd, ask whether it is odd Latin or faithful Latin. Often it is the second: the Latin keeps a Hebrew or Greek idiom that Latin did not have. The Fathers and medieval readers learned this Latin as the language of Scripture, and it shaped later Christian Latin.

The English beside each Vulgate verse in this library is the Douay-Rheims version, a translation made from the Latin. Use it to check your reading, and notice how it too sometimes keeps the Latin's word order.

sections.heading: Hebrew habits in Latin dress
body: Hebrew narrative joins its clauses with a single small word that Latin renders *et*. A Vulgate narrative is therefore a string of short clauses, each beginning *et*: this is called parataxis (clauses set side by side) and it contrasts with the long Roman period in which clauses hang on one another. Treat *et* as a simple joiner: it may be 'and', 'then', 'but' or nothing at all in English, depending on the sentence.

A second Hebrew mark is the formula *et factum est*, which opens an event. Luke 2:15 begins *Et factum est ut discesserunt*, and the real action follows in the next clause. Do not take it as a complete sentence meaning 'and it was done'; it is a signal, close to the old English 'and it came to pass'.

Hebrew often strengthens a verb by putting a verbal noun or infinitive before it. The Vulgate copies this with an ablative noun or a participle of the same root: in Genesis 2:17 the Latin is *morte morieris*, literally 'by death you will die', and in Acts 7:34, quoting the Old Testament, *videns vidi*, 'seeing I have seen'. In both the doubling adds emphasis ('you will surely die', 'I have indeed seen'); it does not mean a different action in each word.

The same habit appears in nouns. 'Son of' and 'children of' mark a person's character or origin: *filius perditionis* in John 17:12 is a person marked by perdition, and *filii Israël* is the Israelites. And Hebrew prepositions that are used for place or direction are rendered literally: *a facie Domini* in Genesis 3:8 is 'from the face of the Lord', which means 'from the presence of' him; *in manu forti* in Exodus 13:9 uses *in* with the ablative for the instrument, 'with a strong hand'.

'From the presence of'; 'by the hand of', 'with'
'That' after a verb of saying or knowing, or a mark of direct speech

sections.heading: Greek habits in Latin dress
body: Classical Latin reports a statement with the accusative and infinitive. The Vulgate very often uses *quia* or *quoniam* with a finite verb instead, following the Greek hoti: in John 1:34 the Baptist 'bore witness *quia hic est Filius Dei*', that this is the Son of God. The reported words keep their own tense and person, as in direct speech. *quia* and *quoniam* also still mean 'because', so only the sentence tells you which.

A related use: *quia* can open the very words someone spoke, like a mark of quotation. In John 1:20, *confessus est: Quia non sum ego Christus*, the Baptist's words follow, and *quia* here is hardly translated.

Greek is fond of participles, and the Vulgate follows. In Luke 2:8 the shepherds are *vigilantes* and *custodientes*, 'watching' and 'keeping', and in 2:16 they come *festinantes*, 'hurrying'. Where Cicero would use a finite verb, a relative clause or a subordinate clause, the Vulgate often uses a participle, and you supply the link (time, manner, cause) from the sense.

sections.heading: How to read a Vulgate sentence
body: First find the finite verbs, then notice each *et*, each participle and each *quia* or *quoniam*. Ask of each: is this ordinary Latin, or does it keep the shape of the source? If it keeps the shape, translate the sense without correcting the Latin.

Do not assume that every unusual phrase is a Hebraism. Scholars who study the Vulgate disagree about particular cases, and some turns of phrase are simply later, simpler Latin. The table lists features that are widely recognised.

misunderstandings: The Vulgate is not 'bad Latin'. It is Latin written to carry a Hebrew or Greek text across, and it has its own regular habits.
*quia* does not always mean 'because'. After a verb of saying, seeing or knowing it often means 'that', and in a quotation it may just introduce the words.
*et* does not always mean 'and'. At the head of a Vulgate clause it is often only a joiner.
*in* with the ablative is not always place. In *in manu forti* it is the instrument, 'with a strong hand'.
A doubled form such as *morte morieris* is not two different acts. It is one act stated emphatically.

deeper.heading: Hebrew by way of Greek
body: A great deal of the Hebrew flavour in the New Testament Latin reached it through Greek. Luke wrote Greek, which had itself been shaped by the Greek Old Testament; the Vulgate then rendered Luke's Greek into Latin. A phrase such as *et factum est* therefore has two earlier lives, in Hebrew and in Greek, before it is Latin.

quoted.title: Luke
quoted.english: And it came to pass, after the angels departed from them into heaven, the shepherds said one to another: Let us go over to Bethlehem, and let us see this word that is come to pass, which the Lord hath shewed to us.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *Et factum est ut discesserunt*: the formula of the Hebrew narrative, 'and it came to pass that they departed', and the real event is in the clause after it. *discesserunt* is a perfect, 3rd person plural: the angels left. The shepherds then speak: *loquebantur* is imperfect, 'were saying', and *Transeamus* is the exhortation 'let us go over'.

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: And I saw, and I gave testimony, that this is the Son of God.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *quia* follows *perhibui* and introduces what was testified: 'that this is the Son of God'. Classical Latin would have *hunc esse Filium Dei*, an accusative and infinitive. The Vulgate uses a finite verb (*est*), as the Greek does, and the tense stays that of the original statement.

examples.analysis: *morte* is ablative singular of *mors* and *morieris* is a future of *morior*: 'you will die'. Together they are *morte morieris*, 'surely die', Hebrew emphasis put into Latin. Notice the English matched with the verse: 'thou shalt die the death'.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the afternoon air, Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord God, amidst the trees of paradise.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *abscondit* is a perfect: they hid. The subject is *Adam et uxor ejus*. The phrase *a facie Domini Dei* is 'from the face of the Lord God', a Hebrew idiom for 'from the presence of'; *facie* is ablative after *a*.

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: While I was with them, I kept them in thy name. Those whom thou gavest me have I kept; and none of them is lost, but the son of perdition, that the scripture may be fulfilled.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *filius perditionis*: *filius* is nominative and *perditionis* genitive. 'Son of' with a noun is a Hebrew way of saying that someone is marked by that thing, so the phrase describes a person, here the one doomed to perdition. The English renders it 'the son of perdition', which keeps the idiom.

options: It is a formula that opens an event: 'and it came to pass that'; the action is in the clause that follows

It introduces the very words that were said, like a mark of quotation

check.prompt: What is the force of *Videns vidi afflictionem populi mei*?

quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: The speaker saw twice, on two separate days
Emphasis: 'I have surely seen', a participle and finite verb of the same root, after Hebrew
The speaker has been seen by someone else
The speaker is uncertain whether he saw it
check.explain: *Videns vidi* is the Hebrew intensifying construction expressed by a participle and a finite verb of the same verb. Compare *morte morieris*.

options: Finite verbs in the imperfect with the shepherds as object

check.explain: They agree with *pastores*. The Vulgate here follows the Greek habit of describing action with participles joined by *et*.

check.prompt: In Luke 2:9 nearly every clause begins with *et* (*Et ecce angelus Domini stetit ... et claritas Dei circumfulsit illos, et timuerunt timore magno*). What is this style?

quoted.title: Luke
quoted.english: And behold an angel of the Lord stood by them, and the brightness of God shone round about them; and they feared with a great fear.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: A list of nouns in the same case
Clauses set side by side with *et*; the Hebrew narrative style, not the Roman period
check.explain: Parataxis, with *et* as a simple joiner. Latin of Cicero's kind would tie the clauses together with subordinate clauses and participles.
